name: Factors Affecting the Rate of Cellular Respiration
what: Covers the three factors that affect the rate of cellular respiration: temperature, glucose availability and oxygen concentration, and explains how each factor influences the rate through its effect on enzyme activity or substrate availability.
why: These factors connect enzyme theory to cellular respiration directly, and are often assessed alongside graphs or experimental scenarios. Understanding them also explains the switch between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in living organisms.

items.title: I can list the factors that affect the rate of cellular respiration
items.what: The three factors that affect the rate of cellular respiration are temperature, glucose availability and oxygen concentration.
items.why: Listing these factors correctly without confusing them with factors affecting photosynthesis is the starting point for more detailed explanation questions.
items.example: A yeast population fermenting grape juice will respire faster as glucose concentration rises, up to the point where the enzymes involved are working at their maximum rate.

items.title: I can explain why and how temperature affects the rate of cellular respiration
items.what: As temperature increases, kinetic energy of molecules increases, leading to more frequent successful collisions between substrates and enzyme active sites, so the rate of respiration rises. Above the optimum temperature, enzymes denature, their active site changes shape and substrates can no longer bind, causing the rate to fall sharply.
items.why: Temperature-rate graphs for cellular respiration follow the same enzyme-based pattern as those for photosynthesis. Being able to explain the shape of the curve using enzyme theory is essential for extended response marks.
items.example: At 37°C (human body temperature), the enzymes of cellular respiration operate near their optimum. If body temperature rises to 42°C during a high fever, enzyme denaturation begins and the rate of cellular respiration decreases.

items.title: I can explain why and how glucose availability affects the rate of cellular respiration
items.what: Glucose is the primary substrate for cellular respiration. As glucose concentration increases, enzyme active sites are occupied more frequently and the rate of respiration rises. At very high glucose concentrations, all enzyme active sites are saturated and the rate plateaus.
items.why: Glucose availability links directly to the concept of substrate concentration from enzyme theory and explains real situations such as post-meal blood glucose spikes or athletic performance.
items.example: A graph of glucose concentration vs rate of cellular respiration shows a curve that rises steeply at low concentrations, then flattens into a plateau when enzyme active sites are fully saturated.

items.title: I can explain why and how oxygen concentration affects the rate of cellular respiration
items.what: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain. As oxygen concentration increases, the rate of the electron transport chain increases, producing more ATP. At very low oxygen levels, aerobic respiration slows and cells switch to anaerobic fermentation, producing only 2 ATP per glucose instead of 30 or 32.
items.why: Understanding the role of oxygen explains why cells switch between aerobic and anaerobic respiration and why aerobic respiration is far more efficient. This is assessed in scenarios involving exercise, sealed containers or low-oxygen environments.
items.example: When nitrogen gas is bubbled through a yeast solution to remove all oxygen, yeast switch to alcoholic fermentation, producing ethanol and CO2 and only 2 ATP per glucose. When oxygen is reintroduced, the rate of CO2 production increases significantly as aerobic respiration resumes.
